n: *Study note:* *Psalm 101*. The psalmist, who appears to be a king, promises to promote justice in his land and vows to rid his royal court of evildoers.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “take notice of.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will walk about in the integrity of my heart in the midst of my house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will not set before my eyes a thing of worthlessness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the doing of swerving [deeds] I hate.” The Hebrew term סֵטִים (setim) is probably an alternate spelling of שֵׂטִים (setim), which appears in many medieval Hebrew mss. The form appears to be derived from a verbal root שׂוּט (sut, “to fall away; to swerve”; see {{Psalm 40:4|Ps 40:4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it [i.e., the doing of evil deeds] does not cling to me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a perverse heart will turn aside from me.” The adjective עִקֵּשׁ (ʿiqqesh) has the basic nuance “twisted; crooked” and by extension refers to someone or something that is morally perverse (see {{Psalm 18:26|Ps 18:26}}). It appears frequently in the Book of Proverbs, where it is used of evil people ({{Proverbs 22:5|22:5}}), speech ({{Proverbs 8:8|8:8}}; {{Proverbs 19:1|19:1}}), thoughts ({{Proverbs 11:20|11:20}}; {{Proverbs 17:20|17:20}}), and life styles ({{Proverbs 2:15|2:15}}; {{Proverbs 28:6|28:6}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “know.” The king will not willingly allow perverse individuals to remain in his royal court.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[one who has] pride of eyes and wideness [i.e., arrogance] of heart, him I will not endure.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my eyes [are] on the faithful of the land.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text simply reads, “in order to live with me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one who walks in the way of integrity, he will minister to me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will not live in the midst of my house, one who does deceit.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one who speaks lies will not be established before my eyes.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 102*. The psalmist laments his oppressed state, but longs for a day when the Lord will restore Jerusalem and vindicate his suffering people.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and may my cry for help come to you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not hide your face from me in the day of my trouble.” The idiom “to hide the face” can mean “to ignore” (see {{Psalm 10:11|Pss 10:11}}; {{Psalm 13:1|13:1}}; {{Psalm 51:9|51:9}}) or carry the stronger idea of “to reject” (see {{Psalm 29:7|Pss 29:7}}; {{Psalm 30:7|30:7}}; {{Psalm 88:14|88:14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “turn toward me your ear.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for my days come to an end in smoke.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun קֵד (qed, “fireplace”) occurs only here, in {{Isaiah 33:14|Isa 33:14}} (where it refers to the fire itself), and perhaps in Lev 6:2.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “struck, attacked.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I forget.”

*Study note:* *I am unable to eat food*. During his time of mourning, the psalmist refrained from eating. In the following verse he describes metaphorically the physical effects of fasting.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the sound of my groaning my bone[s] stick to my flesh.” The preposition at the beginning of the verse is causal; the phrase “sound of my groaning” is metonymic for the anxiety that causes the groaning. The point seems to be this: Anxiety (which causes the psalmist to groan) keeps him from eating (v. {{Psalm 102:4|4}}). This physical deprivation in turn makes him emaciated—he is turned to “skin and bones,” so to speak.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term קָאַת (qaʾat) refers to some type of bird (see Lev 11:18; {{Deuteronomy 14:17|Deut 14:17}}) that was typically found near ruins (see Zeph 2:14). Modern translations have frequently rendered this as some type of owl (NIV, REB “desert owl”; NRSV “owl”).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term כוֹס (khos) refers to a bird (see Lev 11:17; {{Deuteronomy 14:16|Deut 14:16}}), probably a type of owl (cf. NIV, REB “owl”; NRSV “little owl”).

*Study note:* By comparing himself to a *screech owl among the ruins*, the psalmist may be highlighting his loneliness (see v. {{Psalm 102:7|7}}), though he may also be comparing his cries for help to the owl’s screech.

*Translator's note:* This probably refers to the psalmist’s inability to sleep. Another option is to translate, “I keep watch,” in which case it might refer to watching for a response from the Lord (see vv. {{Psalm 102:1|1-2}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by me they swear.” When the psalmist’s enemies call judgment down on others, they hold the psalmist up as a prime example of what they desire their enemies to become.

*Study note:* Mourners would sometimes put *ashes* on their head or roll in ashes as a sign of mourning (see {{2 Samuel 13:19|2 Sam 13:19}}; {{Job 2:8|Job 2:8}}; {{Isaiah 58:5|Isa 58:5}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “weeping.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my days [are] like an extended [or “lengthening”] shadow,” that is, like a late afternoon shadow made by the descending sun that will soon be swallowed up by complete darkness.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sit” (i.e., sit enthroned, see {{Psalm 9:7|Ps 9:7}}). The imperfect verbal form highlights the generalization.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and your remembrance [is] for a generation and a generation.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal forms are understood as expressing the psalmist’s confidence in God’s intervention. Another option is to take them as expressing the psalmist’s request or wish, “You, rise up and have compassion!”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* The Poel of חָנַן (khanan) occurs only here and in {{Proverbs 14:21|Prov 14:21}}, where it refers to having compassion on the poor.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her dust,” probably referring to the dust of the city’s rubble.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will fear the name of the Lord.” To “fear” God’s name means to have a healthy respect for his revealed reputation which in turn motivates one to obey God’s commands (see {{Psalm 86:11|Ps 86:11}}).

*Translator's note:* The verb “will fear” is understood by ellipsis in the second line (see the preceding line).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew adjective עַרְעָר (ʿarar, “destitute”) occurs only here in the OT. It is derived from the verbal root ערר (“to strip oneself”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “despise.”

*Translator's note:* The perfect verbal forms in vv. {{Psalm 102:16|16-17}} are functioning as future perfects, indicating future actions that will precede the future developments described in v. {{Psalm 102:15|15}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has simply “this,” referring to the anticipated divine intervention on behalf of Zion (vv. {{Psalm 102:13|13}}, {{Psalm 102:16|16-17}}). The referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* Or “created.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the height of his sanctuary.”

*Translator's note:* The perfect verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 102:19|19}} are functioning as future perfects, indicating future actions that will precede the future developments described in v. {{Psalm 102:18|18}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the sons of death.” The phrase “sons of death” (see also {{Psalm 79:11|Ps 79:11}}) is idiomatic for those condemned to die.
*Translator's note:* “and the kingdoms to serve the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he has afflicted my strength in the way.” The term “way” refers here to the course of the psalmist’s life, which appears to be ending prematurely (vv. {{Psalm 102:23|23b-24}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not lift me up in the middle of my days.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in a generation of generations [are] your years.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stand.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb חָלַף (khalaf) occurs twice in this line, once in the Hiphil (“you will remove them”) and once in the Qal (“they will disappear”). The repetition draws attention to the statement.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you [are] he,” or “you [are] the one.” The statement may echo the Lord’s affirmation “I am he” in {{Isaiah 41:4|Isa 41:4}}; {{Isaiah 43:10|43:10}}, {{Isaiah 43:13|13}}; {{Isaiah 46:10|46:10}}; {{Isaiah 48:12|48:12}}. In each of these passages the affirmation emphasizes the fact that the Lord transcends time limitations, the very point being made in {{Psalm 102:27|Ps 102:27}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “offspring”; *Heb* “seed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “before you will be established.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 103*. The psalmist praises God for his mercy and willingness to forgive his people.

*Translator's note:* The verb “praise” is understood by ellipsis in the second line (see the preceding line).
*Translator's note:* Or “his benefits” (see 2 Chr 32:25, where the noun is also used of kind deeds performed by the Lord).
*Translator's note:* This relatively rare noun refers to deadly diseases (see {{Deuteronomy 29:22|Deut 29:22}}; Jer 14:18; 16:4; 2 Chr 21:19).

*Translator's note:* Or “redeems.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term שַׁחַת (shakhat, “pit”) is often used as a title for Sheol (see {{Psalm 16:10|Pss 16:10}}; {{Psalm 30:9|30:9}}; {{Psalm 49:9|49:9}}; 55:24 HT [{{Psalm 55:23|55:23}} ET]).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “who satisfies with the good of your ornaments.” The text as it stands makes little, if any, sense. The translation assumes an emendation of עֶדְיֵךְ (ʿedyekh, “your ornaments”) to עֹדֵכִי (ʿodekhi, “your duration; your continuance”), that is, “your life” (see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* [WBC], 18).

*Study note:* The expression *your youth is renewed like an eagle’s* may allude to the phenomenon of molting, whereby the *eagle* grows new feathers.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord does fairness, and [acts of] justice for all the oppressed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “made known his ways.” God’s “ways” in this context are his protective and salvific acts in fulfillment of his promise (see also {{Deuteronomy 32:4|Deut 32:4}}; {{Psalm 18:30|Pss 18:30}}; {{Psalm 67:2|67:2}}; {{Psalm 77:13|77:13}} [note vv. {{Psalm 77:11|11-12}}, {{Psalm 77:14|14}}]; {{Psalm 138:5|138:5}}; {{Psalm 145:17|145:17}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “slow to anger” (see {{Psalm 86:15|Ps 86:15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and great of loyal love” (see {{Psalm 86:15|Ps 86:15}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb נָטַר (natar) is usually taken to mean “to keep; to guard,” with “anger” being understood by ellipsis. The idiom “to guard anger” is then understood to mean “to remain angry” (see Lev 19:18; Jer 3:5, 12; Nah 1:2). However, it is possible that this is a homonymic root meaning “to be angry” (see *HALOT* 695 s.v. נטר).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “not according to our sins does he do to us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and not according to our misdeeds does he repay us.”

*Translator's note:* For this sense of the verb גָבַר (gavar), see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 17, 19.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who fear him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sunrise.”

*Translator's note:* Or “sunset.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term פֶּשַׁע (peshaʿ, rebellious act”) is here used metonymically for the guilt such actions produce.

*Translator's note:* Or “sons,” but the Hebrew term sometimes refers to children in general.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who fear him.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[as for] mankind, like grass [are] his days.” The Hebrew noun אֱנוֹשׁ (ʾenosh) is used here generically of human beings. What is said is true of all mankind.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the] wind.” The word “hot” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but the loyal love of the Lord [is] from everlasting to everlasting over those who fear him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his righteousness to sons of sons.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to those who remember his precepts to do them.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[you] mighty ones of strength, doers of his word, by listening to the voice of his word.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all his hosts.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his attendants, doers of his desire.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all his works,” which includes mankind.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “places.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 104*. The psalmist praises God as the ruler of the world who sustains all life.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “very great.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one who lays the beams on water [in] his upper rooms.” The “water” mentioned here corresponds to the “waters above” mentioned in {{Genesis 1:7|Gen 1:7}}. For a discussion of the picture envisioned by the psalmist, see L. I. J. Stadelmann, *The Hebrew Conception of the World*, 44-45.

*Study note:* Verse {{Psalm 104:3|3}} may depict the Lord riding a cherub, which is in turn propelled by the *wind* current. Another option is that the *wind* is personified as a cherub. See {{Psalm 18:10|Ps 18:10}} and the discussion of ancient Near Eastern parallels to the imagery in M. Weinfeld, “‘Rider of the Clouds’ and ‘Gatherer of the Clouds’,” *JANESCU* 5 (1973): 422-24.

*Study note:* In Ugaritic mythology Yam’s messengers appear as *flaming fire* before the assembly of the gods. See G. R. Driver, *Canaanite Myths and Legends*, 42.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and his attendants a flaming fire.” The lack of agreement between the singular “fire” and plural “attendants” has prompted various emendations. Some read “fire and flame.” The present translation assumes an emendation from מְשָׁרְתָיו (mesharetayv, “his attendants”) to מְשָׁרְתוֹ (meshareto, “his attendant”), a reading supported by one of the Dead Sea Scrolls, 4Q93.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “you covered it.” The masculine suffix is problematic if the grammatically feminine noun “earth” is the antecedent. For this reason some emend the form from כִּסִּיתוֹ (kissito) to a feminine verb with feminine suffix, כִּסַּתָּה (kissattah, “[the watery deep] covered it [i.e., the earth]”), a reading assumed by the present translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stood.”

*Study note:* Verse {{Psalm 104:6|6}} refers to the condition described in {{Genesis 1:2|Gen 1:2}} (note the use of the Hebrew term תְּהוֹם [tehom, “watery deep”] in both texts).

*Study note:* Verses {{Psalm 104:7|7-8}} poetically depict {{Genesis 1:9|Gen 1:9-10}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from your shout they fled, from the sound of your thunder they hurried off.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a boundary you set up, they will not cross, they will not return to cover the earth.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the] one who sends springs into streams.” Another option is to translate, “he sends streams [i.e., streams that originate from springs] into the valleys” (cf. NIV).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “among the thick foliage they give a sound.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from his upper rooms.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the fruit of your works the earth is full.” The translation assumes that “fruit” is literal here. If “fruit” is understood more abstractly as “product; result,” then one could translate, “the earth flourishes as a result of your deeds” (cf. NIV, NRSV, REB).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “causes the grass to sprout up.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for the service of man” (see {{Genesis 2:5|Gen 2:5}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to cause food to come out from the earth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and wine [that] makes the heart of man happy.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to make [the] face shine from oil.” The Hebrew verb צָהַל (tsahal, “to shine”) occurs only here in the OT. It appears to be an alternate form of צָהַר (tsahar), a derivative from צָהָרִים (tsaharim, “noon”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and food [that] sustains the heart of man.”

*Study note:* *The trees of the* Lord are the cedars of Lebanon (see the next line), which are viewed as special because of their great size and grandeur. The Lebanon forest was viewed elsewhere in the OT as the “garden of God” (see {{Ezekiel 31:8|Ezek 31:8}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “are satisfied,” which means here that they receive abundant rain (see v. {{Psalm 104:13|13}}).

*Study note:* The cedars and *evergreens* of the Lebanon forest are frequently associated (see, for example, 2 Chr 2:8; {{Isaiah 14:8|Isa 14:8}}; {{Isaiah 37:24|37:24}}; {{Ezekiel 31:8|Ezek 31:8}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the] heron [in the] evergreens [is] its home.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the high mountains [are] for the goats.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he made [the] moon for appointed times.” The phrase “appointed times” probably refers to the months of the Hebrew lunar calendar.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* more metaphorically, “knows its setting.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you make darkness, so that it might be night.”
*Study note:* The lions’ roaring is viewed as a request for *food from God*.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “man goes out to his work, and to his labor until evening.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “How many [are] your works, O Lord.” In this case the Lord’s “works” are the creatures he has made, as the preceding and following contexts make clear.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all of them with wisdom you have made.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this [is] the sea, great and broad of hands [i.e., “sides” or “shores”].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “where [there are] swimming things, and without number.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[and] this Leviathan, [which] you formed to play in it.” Elsewhere Leviathan is a multiheaded sea monster that symbolizes forces hostile to God (see {{Psalm 74:14|Ps 74:14}}; {{Isaiah 27:1|Isa 27:1}}), but here it appears to be an actual marine creature created by God, probably some type of whale.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “All of them.” The pronoun “them” refers not just to the sea creatures mentioned in vv. {{Psalm 104:25|25-26}}, but to all living things (see v. {{Psalm 104:24|24}}). This has been specified in the translation as “all of your creatures” for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to give their food in its time.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you hide your face, they are terrified.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “be forever.”

*Translator's note:* Or “rejoice in his works.”
*Translator's note:* That is, the psalmist’s thoughts as expressed in his songs of praise.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the judgments of his mouth.”

*Translator's note:* Or “offspring”; *Heb* “seed.”

*Text-critical note:* Some mss have “Israel,” which appears in the parallel version of this psalm in 1 Chr 16:13.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sons.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in all the earth [are] his judgments.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the] word he commanded.” The text refers here to God’s unconditional covenantal promise to Abraham and the patriarchs, as vv. {{Psalm 105:10|10-12}} make clear.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and from a kingdom to another nation.”

*Translator's note:* The word “saying” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “anointed.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and every staff of food he broke.” The psalmist refers to the famine that occurred in Joseph’s time (see v. {{Psalm 105:17|17}} and {{Genesis 41:53|Gen 41:53-57}}).
*Translator's note:* After the reference to the famine in v. {{Psalm 105:16|16}}, v. {{Psalm 105:17|17}} flashes back to events that preceded the famine (see {{Genesis 37|Gen 37}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they afflicted his feet with shackles.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his neck came [into] iron.” The Hebrew term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) with the suffix could mean simply “he” or “his life.” But the nuance “neck” makes good sense here (note the reference to his “feet” in the preceding line). See L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 38.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “word,” probably referring to Joseph’s prediction about the fate of Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker (see {{Genesis 41:9|Gen 41:9-14}}).

*Translator's note:* This line may refer to Joseph’s prediction of the famine in response to Pharaoh’s dream. Joseph emphasized to Pharaoh that the interpretation of the dream came from God (see {{Genesis 41:16|Gen 41:16}}, {{Genesis 41:25|25}}, {{Genesis 41:28|28}}, {{Genesis 41:32|32}}, {{Genesis 41:39|39}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “refined him.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the] king sent and set him free.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he made him master of his house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to bind his officials by his will.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his elders he taught wisdom.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “entered.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lived as a resident foreigner.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him,” referring to “his people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his,” referring to “his people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their heart.”

*Translator's note:* Or “to deal deceptively.” The Hitpael of נָכַל (nakhal) occurs only here and in {{Genesis 37:18|Gen 37:18}}, where it is used of Joseph’s brothers “plotting” to kill him.
*Translator's note:* Apparently the pronoun refers to “his servants” (i.e., the Israelites, see v. {{Psalm 105:25|25}}).

*Study note:* *He made it dark*. The psalmist begins with the ninth plague (see {{Exodus 10:21|Exod 10:21-29}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he sent darkness and made it dark.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they did not rebel against his words.” Apparently this refers to Moses and Aaron, who obediently carried out God’s orders.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he gave their rains hail.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fire of flames [was] in their land.”

*Study note:* Verses {{Psalm 105:28|28-36}} recall the plagues in a different order than the one presented in Exodus: v. {{Psalm 105:28|28}} (plague 9), v. {{Psalm 105:29|29}} (plague 1), v. {{Psalm 105:30|30}} (plague 2), v. {{Psalm 105:31|31a}} (plague 4), v. {{Psalm 105:31|31b}} (plague 3), vv. {{Psalm 105:32|32-33}} (plague 7), vv. {{Psalm 105:34|34-35}} (plague 8), v. {{Psalm 105:36|36}} (plague 10). No reference is made in {{Psalm 105|Ps 105}} to plagues 5 and 6.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the beginning of all their strength,” that is, reproductive power (see {{Psalm 78:51|Ps 78:51}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “them”; the referent (the Lord’s people) has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The word “enriched” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for fear of them had fallen upon them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he [i.e., his people] asked.” The singular form should probably be emended to a plural שָׁאֲלוּ (shaʾalu, “they asked”), the ו (vav) having fallen off by haplography (note the vav at the beginning of the following form).

*Translator's note:* Or “bread of heaven.” The reference is to manna (see {{Exodus 16:4|Exod 16:4}}, {{Exodus 16:13|13-15}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he led his people out with joy, with a ringing cry, his chosen ones.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the [product of the] work of peoples they possessed.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 106*. The psalmist recalls Israel’s long history of rebellion against God, despite his mighty saving deeds on their behalf.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for forever [is] his loyal love.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[or] cause to be heard all his praise.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “good.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in order that [I may] rejoice with the rejoicing of your nation.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with your inheritance.”

*Study note:* *They rebelled*. The psalmist recalls the people’s complaint recorded in {{Exodus 14:12|Exod 14:12}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Reed Sea” (also in vv. {{Psalm 106:9|9}}, {{Psalm 106:22|22}}). “Reed Sea” (or “Sea of Reeds”) is a more accurate rendering of the Hebrew expression יָם סוּף (yam suf), traditionally translated “Red Sea.” See the note on the term “Red Sea” in {{Exodus 13:18|Exod 13:18}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his name,” which here stands metonymically for God’s reputation.

*Study note:* *They had an insatiable craving*. This is described in {{Numbers 11:4|Num 11:4-35}}.

*Study note:* In vv. {{Psalm 109:6|6-19}} the psalmist calls on God to judge his enemies severely. Some attribute this curse-list to the psalmist’s enemies rather than the psalmist. In this case one should paraphrase v. {{Psalm 109:6|6}}: “They say about me, ‘Appoint an evil man, etc.’” Those supporting this line of interpretation point out that vv. {{Psalm 109:2|2-5}} and {{Psalm 109:20|20}} refer to the enemies’ attack on the psalmist being a verbal one. Furthermore in vv. {{Psalm 109:1|1-5}}, {{Psalm 109:20|20}} the psalmist speaks of his enemies in the plural, while vv. {{Psalm 109:6|6-19}} refer to an individual. This use of the singular in vv. {{Psalm 109:6|6-19}} could be readily explained if this is the psalmist’s enemies’ curse on him. However, it is much more natural to understand vv. {{Psalm 109:6|6-19}} as the psalmist’s prayer against his enemies. There is no introductory quotation formula in v. {{Psalm 109:6|6}} to indicate that the psalmist is quoting anyone, and the statement “may the Lord repay my accusers in this way” in v. {{Psalm 109:20|20}} most naturally appears to be a fitting conclusion to the prayer in vv. {{Psalm 109:6|6-19}}. But what about the use of the singular in vv. {{Psalm 109:6|6-19}}? Often in the psalms the psalmist will describe his enemies as a group, but then speak of them as an individual as well, as if viewing his adversaries collectively as one powerful foe. See, for example, {{Psalm 7|Ps 7}}, where the psalmist uses both the plural (vv. {{Psalm 109:1|1}}, {{Psalm 109:6|6}}) and the singular (vv. {{Psalm 109:2|2}}, {{Psalm 109:4|4-5}}) in referring to enemies. Perhaps by using the singular in such cases, the psalmist wants to single out each enemy for individual attention, or perhaps he has one especially hostile enemy in mind who epitomizes the opposition of the whole group. This may well be the case in {{Psalm 109|Ps 109}}. Perhaps we should understand the singular throughout vv. 6-19 in the sense of “each and every one.” For a lengthy and well-reasoned defense of the opposite view—that vv. {{Psalm 109:6|6-19}} are a quotation of what the enemies said about the psalmist—see L. *Study note:* A *curse* in OT times consists of a formal appeal to God to bring judgment down upon another. Curses were sometimes justified (such as the one spoken by the psalmist here in vv. {{Psalm 109:6|6-19}}), but when they were not, the one pronouncing the curse was in danger of bringing the anticipated judgment down upon himself.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he loved a curse and it came [upon] him.” A reference to the evil man experiencing a curse seems premature here, for the psalmist is asking God to bring judgment on his enemies. For this reason some (cf. NIV, NRSV) prefer to repoint the vav (ו) on “it came” as conjunctive and translate the verb as a jussive of prayer (“may it come upon him!”). The prefixed form with vav consecutive in the next line is emended in the same way and translated, “may it be far from him.” However, the psalmist may be indicating that the evil man’s lifestyle has already begun to yield its destructive fruit.

For him cursing was as refreshing as drinking water or massaging oneself with oil. Another option is that the destructive effects of a curse are in view. In this case a destructive curse invades his very being, like water or oil. Some who interpret the verse this way prefer to repoint the verb from the preterite form וַתָּבֹא (vattavoʾ, “and it came”) to a jussive form וְתָבֹא (vetavoʾ, “and may it come!”).

*Study note:* *Psalm 110*. In this royal psalm the psalmist announces God’s oracle to the Davidic king. The first part of the oracle appears in v. 1, the second in v. 4. In vv. 2-3 the psalmist addresses the king, while in vv. 5-7 he appears to address God.

*Translator's note:* The word נְאֻם (neʾum) is used frequently in the OT of a formal divine announcement through a prophet.

*Study note:* *My lord*. In the psalm’s original context the speaker is an unidentified prophetic voice in the royal court, likely addressing David, the head of the dynasty. In the course of time the psalm is applied to each successive king in the dynasty, and is likely understood as such by David (see {{2 Samuel 7:11|2 Sam 7:11-14}}, {{2 Samuel 7:19|19}}). Since the Psalm as a whole is attributed to David, it is appropriate to speak of any of its parts as coming from him, whether he composed them, reported them, or commissioned them. Ultimately these words come to apply to the ideal Davidic king, specifically Jesus Christ, the Son of David. Thus, in the irony of the incarnation, the lord who receives the promise is the Lord who made the promise. This creates some complexity in typographic convention, as NET chooses to use lower case here in the Psalm (“my lord”) due to its original context, even though we now know it to be ultimately fulfilled by our Lord. The Greek translation introduces more difficulty because it uses κύριος (kurios, “lord”) for both the Lord’s name, יהוה (YHWH, probably pronounced “Yahweh”) and the title אֲדוֹנַי (ʾadonay, “Lord”) (the word here is not the title, but simply “lord” [אָדוֺן, ʾadon] with the suffix “my”). This complexity and irony are the grounds for the riddle posed by Jesus in the gospels ({{Matthew 22:43|Matt 22:43-45}}; {{Mark 12:36|Mark 12:36-37}}; Luke 20:42-44), which the Pharisees could not solve because they were not expecting the Davidic lord to be the Lord. Peter incorporates the answer “that God has made this Jesus whom you crucified both Lord and Christ” into his sermon at Pentecost ({{Acts 2:34|Acts 2:34-35}}).

*Study note:* To sit at the “right hand” of the king was an honor (see {{1 Kings 2:19|1 Kgs 2:19}}). The Lord’s invitation to the Davidic king to *sit down* at his *right hand* reflects the king’s position as the Lord’s vice-regent. In Ugaritic myth (*CTA* 4 v. 108-10) the artisan god Kothar-wa-Khasis is described as sitting at the right hand of the storm god Baal. See G. R. Driver, *Canaanite Myths and Legends*, 61-62.

*Study note:* When the Lord made his covenant with David, he promised to subdue the king’s *enemies* (see {{2 Samuel 7:9|2 Sam 7:9-11}}; {{Psalm 89:22|Ps 89:22-23}}).

*Translator's note:* Since the Lord is mentioned in the third person (note the use of the first person in v. {{Psalm 110:1|1}}), it is likely that these are the psalmist’s words to the king, not a continuation of the oracle per se.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is understood here as descriptive-dramatic or as generalizing, though it could be taken as future.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “in splendor of holiness.” The plural construct form הַדְרֵי (hadre, from הָדַר, hadar, “splendor”) occurs only here; it may indicate degree or perhaps refer by metonymy to garments (see {{Psalm 29:2|Pss 29:2}} and {{Psalm 96:9|96:9}}, where the phrase הַדְרַת קֹדֶשׁ [hadrat qodesh] refers to “holy attire”). If one retains the reading of the MT, this phrase should probably be taken with the preceding line. However, because of the subsequent references to “dawn” and to “dew,” it is better to emend the text to הַרְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ (harere qodesh, “mountains of holiness”), a reading found in many medieval Hebrew mss and in some other ancient witnesses (see Joel 2:2; {{Psalm 133:3|Ps 133:3}}, as well as L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* [WBC], 80). The “mountains of holiness” are probably the hills surrounding Zion (see {{Psalm 87:1|Pss 87:1}}; {{Psalm 125:2|125:2}}; {{Psalm 133:3|133:3}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the womb of dawn.” The Hebrew noun רֶחֶם (rekhem, “womb”) is probably used here metonymically for “birth.” The form מִשְׁחָר (mishkhar) occurs only here and should be emended to שַׁחַר (shakhar, “dawn”) with the מ (mem) being understood as a duplication of the mem ending the preceding word. The phrase “womb [i.e., “birth”] of dawn” refers to sunrise.

*Study note:* The point of the metaphor is not entirely clear. The *dew* may symbolize the king’s youthful vitality or, more likely (note the parallelism), may refer to his army of strong, youthful warriors.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to you [is].”

*Translator's note:* Or “swears, vows.”

*Translator's note:* Or “will not change his mind.” The negated Niphal imperfect of נָחַם (nakham) is a way of marking an announcement as an irrevocable decree. See {{1 Samuel 15:29|1 Sam 15:29}}; {{Ezekiel 24:14|Ezek 24:14}}, as well as R. B. Chisholm, “Does God ‘Change His Mind’?” *BSac* 152 (1995): 387-99.

*Study note:* *You are an eternal priest*. The Davidic king exercised a non-Levitical priestly role. The king superintended Judah’s cultic ritual, had authority over the Levites, and sometimes led in formal worship. David himself instructed the Levites to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:11-15), joined the procession, offered sacrifices, wore a priestly ephod, and blessed the people ({{2 Samuel 6:12|2 Sam 6:12-19}}). At the dedication of the temple Solomon led the ceremony, offering sacrifices and praying on behalf of the people ({{1 Kings 8|1 Kgs 8}}).

*Translator's note:* The phrase עַל־דִּבְרָתִי (ʿal divrati) is a variant of עַל־דִּבְרָת (ʿal divrat; the final י [yod] being an archaic genitive ending), which in turn is a variant of עַל דָּבַר (ʿal davar). Both phrases can mean “concerning” or “because of,” but neither of these nuances fits the use of עַל־דִּבְרָתִי in {{Psalm 110:4|Ps 110:4}}. Here the phrase probably carries the sense “according to the manner of.” See L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 81.

*Study note:* The Davidic king’s priestly role is analogous to that of *Melchizedek*, who was both “king of Salem” (i.e., Jerusalem) and a “priest of God Most High” in the time of Abraham ({{Genesis 14:18|Gen 14:18-20}}). Like Melchizedek, the Davidic king was a royal priest, distinct from the Aaronic line (see {{Hebrews 7|Heb 7}}). The analogy focuses on the king’s priestly role; the language need not imply that Melchizedek himself was “an eternal priest.”

*Translator's note:* The MT reads אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay, “Lord”), which in this form to God. Many medieval Hebrew mss read יְהוָה (Yehwah, “Lord”) here. The present translation assumes that the psalmist here addresses the Lord as he celebrates what the king is able to accomplish while positioned at God’s “right hand.” According to this view the king is the subject of the third person verb forms in vv. {{Psalm 110:5|5b-7}}. (2) Another option is to understand the king as the addressee (as in vv. {{Psalm 110:2|2-3}}). In this case “the Lord” is the subject of the third person verbs throughout vv. {{Psalm 110:5|5-7}} and is depicted as a warrior in a very anthropomorphic manner. In this case the Lord is pictured as being at the psalmist’s right hand (just the opposite of v. {{Psalm 110:1|1}}). See {{Psalm 16:8|Pss 16:8}}; {{Psalm 121:5|121:5}}. (3) A third option is to revocalize אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay, “Lord” a reference to God) as אֲדֹנִי (ʾadoni, “my lord”; see v. {{Psalm 110:1|1}}). In this case one may translate, “My lord, at his [God’s] right hand, strikes down.” In this case the king is the subject of the third person verbs in vv. {{Psalm 110:5|5b-7}}.

*Translator's note:* The perfect verbal forms in vv. {{Psalm 110:5|5-6}} are understood here as descriptive-dramatic or as generalizing. Another option is to take them as rhetorical. In this case the psalmist describes anticipated events as if they had already taken place.
